turns.text: how do i reverse a list in python

<|par|>Use the <|bold|>reverse()</|bold|> method to reverse in-place, or the <|bold|>reversed()</|bold|> function to return an iterator:<|/par|><|codeblock|lang='python'|>my_list = [1, 2, 3, 4]
my_list.reverse()
print(my_list)  # [4, 3, 2, 1]
<|/codeblock|><|par|>There's also slicing: <|code|>my_list[::-1]</|code|> returns a reversed copy without modifying the original.<|/par|>

what's the difference between git merge and git rebase? when should i use each

<|thinking|>This is a common source of confusion. Merge preserves history with a merge commit; rebase rewrites it linearly. The rule of thumb is: rebase personal branches, merge shared ones. I'll structure this under headings for clarity.<|/thinking|><|heading|>Core difference<|/heading|><|par|><|bold|>Merge</|bold|> creates a merge commit and keeps the full branch history. <|bold|>Rebase</|bold|> replays your commits on top of the target branch, producing a linear history.<|/par|><|heading|>When to use each<|/heading|><|list|><|item|>Use <|bold|>merge</|bold|> for shared branches — it preserves context the team can see later.<|/item|><|item|>Use <|bold|>rebase</|bold|> on your own feature branch before opening a PR to keep history tidy.<|/item|><|/list|><|par|>Never rebase a branch others have already pulled from — it rewrites shared history.<|/par|>

what does chmod 755 mean in linux

<|heading|>Permission breakdown<|/heading|><|par|>755 is a three-digit octal code. Each digit represents owner / group / everyone:<|/par|><|list|><|item|><|bold|>7</|bold|> (owner) = read + write + execute<|/item|><|item|><|bold|>5</|bold|> (group) = read + execute<|/item|><|item|><|bold|>5</|bold|> (others) = read + execute<|/item|><|/list|><|par|>It's standard for scripts and directories — anyone can use them but only the owner can modify them.<|/par|>

train a leaves at 2pm going 60mph. train b leaves at 3pm from the same station going 75mph on the same track. when does b catch a

<|thinking|>Classic relative-speed problem. Train A has a 1-hour head start (60 miles). Relative speed is 15 mph. 60/15 = 4 hours, so B catches up at 3pm + 4h = 7pm. I'll break it into steps for clarity.<|/thinking|><|heading|>Head start<|/heading|><|par|>By 3pm, train A has traveled <|bold|>60 miles</|bold|> (60 mph × 1 hour).<|/par|><|heading|>Catch-up rate<|/heading|><|par|>Train B gains <|bold|>15 miles per hour</|bold|> (75 − 60).<|/par|><|heading|>Time to catch up<|/heading|><|par|>60 miles ÷ 15 mph = <|bold|>4 hours</|bold|>. So train B catches train A at <|bold|>7:00 pm</|bold|>.<|/par|>
